name: Powell-Cotton Museum, Quex House & Gardens
summary: Victorian explorer's museum of African and Asian animal dioramas and cultural objects, with a family manor house and walled garden.
description: Quex Park, on the southern edge of Birchington, has had a house on it since the early 15th century. The present Regency mansion replaced the older building in the early 19th century, and the estate passed down through the Powell and later Powell-Cotton families. Major Percy Powell-Cotton, born in 1866, founded a museum here in 1896 to show the animals and objects he brought back from long expeditions across Africa and Asia, some lasting a year and a half. The animals were mounted by the famous taxidermist Rowland Ward and are displayed in large habitat scenes across three galleries holding more than 500 specimens. Other rooms cover African artefacts, European firearms and edged weapons, European and Chinese porcelain, and archaeology from Thanet and East Kent, including Bronze Age finds from the Minnis Bay foreshore. A single day ticket also covers Quex House, a family home shaped over generations and shown on guided tours, and the gardens with lawns, a woodland walk and a historic walled kitchen garden. During the First World War the house served as an auxiliary military hospital. The house, the Gun Tower and the Waterloo Tower in the grounds are all Grade II listed.
address: Quex Park, Park Lane, Birchington, Kent
opening_hours: 2026 season 14 Feb - 1 Nov: term time Fri-Sun and bank holidays 11:00-16:00; school holidays Wed-Sun 11:00-16:00; Tuesdays closed. Festive weekends 21 Nov - 13 Dec. Check website.
price: Adult £9, concession £8, child 4-16 £7, under 4 free (2026, per local press; confirm on the museum's booking page). Ticket gives same-day re-entry.
accessibility: The museum publishes an AccessAble guide with detailed access information.
tips: Combine with lunch at Quex Barn next door and a look at the Waterloo Tower in the park. Train: two stops from Margate to Birchington-on-Sea.

name: Waterloo Tower, Quex Park
summary: Regency red-brick bell tower with an iron spire, built by a bell-ringing squire and the first twelve-bell tower in Kent.
description: Rising above the trees of Quex Park, the Waterloo Tower is one of Thanet's oddest landmarks: a secular bell tower built purely for the love of change ringing. John Powell Powell, owner of Quex and an enthusiastic ringer, put it up around 1818-1820 (usually dated 1819) and named it after the Battle of Waterloo. It was the first tower in Kent to hold a ring of twelve bells; they were cast by Thomas Mears at the Whitechapel foundry in London and the heaviest weighs about 15 hundredweight. The square brick section is roughly 66 feet tall and is topped by a later openwork cast-iron spire of almost the same height again. At its foot is a mausoleum dedicated in 1896 to Henry Horace Powell-Cotton. The tower is Grade II listed, and science-fiction fans may recognise it from an episode of the BBC series Blake's 7. The Quex Ringers keep a website about the tower and its bells.
address: Quex Park, Manston Road side, Birchington, Kent
tips: Best seen from the Quex Park grounds or from Manston Road; interior access was not confirmed.

name: Quex Barn Farm Shop & Restaurant
summary: Award-winning estate farm shop with butcher, fishmonger and deli counters, a restaurant and a pizzeria at Quex Park.
description: On the Quex Park estate, a short walk from the Powell-Cotton Museum, Quex Barn is a farm shop and eatery built around local produce. Inside you will find counters for fresh meat, fish and seafood, a cheese and deli counter, and vegetables from the farm. The restaurant cooks with what the shop sells, there is a cafe for coffee and cake, and an Italian pizzeria serves pizzas to eat in or take away later in the week. It was named Farm Shop of the Year in the Kent Life Food and Drink Awards 2019. It is a handy stop for breakfast or lunch before or after visiting the museum and gardens, or for picking up picnic supplies on the way to Minnis Bay.
address: Quex Park Estate, Park Lane, Birchington, Kent
opening_hours: As listed by Visit Thanet: farm shop & cafe Sun-Mon 09:00-17:00, Tue-Sat 09:00-17:30; restaurant daily 09:00-15:00; pizzeria Thu-Sat 13:00-19:30. Check website.
dogs: Visit Thanet lists pets as welcome; assistance dogs welcome.
tips: Pairs naturally with a museum visit; coach and car parking on site.

name: All Saints' Church, Birchington
summary: Birchington's oldest building: a medieval flint church with Thanet's only ancient shingled spire and the Quex family chapel.
description: All Saints stands beside the Square in the middle of the village and is its oldest standing building. It probably began as a chapel of ease under Monkton. The chancel was rebuilt around 1250, when the owners of Quex added the north (Quex) chapel and the monks of Monkton a south-east tower and chapel; the nave was widened around 1350 and the south porch added about 1430. The spire on the tower is the only old shingled spire left in Thanet. Sailors used it as a sea mark, Trinity House paid towards its repair in 1864, it was last re-shingled in 1968 in Canadian red cedar, and an arrow-shaped vane dated 1699 sits on top. The tower holds eight bells, the oldest from 1633, and the clock marked Queen Victoria's 1887 Jubilee. Inside, look for the Quex Chapel with monuments in brass, alabaster and marble from the early 15th century onwards, a brass to a vicar who died in 1523, the 1883 painted reredos, and the memorial windows to Dante Gabriel Rossetti, who is buried in the churchyard.
address: Kent Gardens / The Square, Birchington, Kent
tips: Rossetti's grave is by the south porch; see the church website for service times before visiting the interior.

name: Grave of Dante Gabriel Rossetti
summary: Pre-Raphaelite painter-poet Rossetti died in Birchington in 1882; his Celtic-cross headstone was designed by Ford Madox Brown.
description: In February 1882 the painter and poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti, a founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, came to a bungalow at Birchington hoping the sea air would restore his failing health. He died there that April, on or around Easter Sunday (sources give 9 or 10 April), and was buried in the churchyard of All Saints, close to the south porch. His sister, the poet Christina Rossetti, and his old friend Ford Madox Brown had both visited during his last illness. Brown designed the grave marker, an Irish-style Celtic cross in Portland stone made in 1883-84, with St Luke and an ox carved near its base; the tomb is listed. Inside the church, a pair of memorial windows remembers him: one reproduces a Rossetti painting, the other was designed by his friend Frederic Shields. Birchington Heritage Trust keeps a file on Rossetti in its archive at the library.
address: All Saints' churchyard, The Square, Birchington, Kent
opening_hours: Churchyard visible at any reasonable time
tips: Look by the south porch of the church; pair with the memorial windows inside.

name: The Square, Birchington village centre
summary: The old heart of Birchington, beside All Saints' Church, with cafes and shops leading down Station Road to the sea.
description: The Square is where the old village of Birchington grew up around its medieval church. The name itself goes back to 1240, when the place was recorded as Birchenton, a farmstead among birch trees. In 1565 royal commissioners counted just 42 houses here, and before the 19th century the coast was a haunt of smugglers; some older houses are said to keep cellars and bricked-up tunnels. The arrival of the railway in 1863 and the Railway Hotel (now the Sea View Hotel) two years later turned Birchington into a seaside resort, and Station Road became the main shopping street linking the Square with the station and the bays. Today the Square is a small, busy centre with cafes, pubs and shops, a good starting point for the church and Rossetti's grave and for the walk north to the cliffs.
tips: The A28 runs through the Square, so cross with care.

name: Birchington Heritage Museum (Burley Gallery)
summary: Free local-history museum and archive inside Birchington Library, run by the volunteer Birchington Heritage Trust.
description: The Birchington Heritage Trust keeps its museum and archive room in the Burley Gallery at Birchington Library, having moved there from its old base in The Centre. On display is a selection of objects from the Trust's collection, while the archive holds more than 200 lever-arch files of photographs, maps, objects and notes on every aspect of the parish, arranged A to Z from Acol to York Terrace. Topics include All Saints Church, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, the village windmills, Spurgeon's Homes, both World Wars and the actress Gladys Cooper. Researchers can consult transcripts of the church registers from 1538 and churchwardens' accounts from 1531, poor-law and way-warden accounts, and parish maps dating from 1414 onwards. It is a good rainy-day stop and the place to ask about family or house history.
address: Burley Gallery, Birchington Library, Alpha Road, Birchington, Kent
opening_hours: Museum open during library opening hours; archives staffed Mon (not bank holidays), Thu and Sat 09:30-12:30.
tips: Visit on a Monday, Thursday or Saturday morning if you want to use the archive.

name: Birchington-on-Sea railway station
summary: Southeastern station on the Chatham Main Line, opened 1863; about 1 hr 40 min from London.
description: Birchington's station opened in 1863 and was the spark that turned the farming village into a seaside resort. It sits on the Chatham Main Line and trains are run by Southeastern, with journeys to London taking around an hour and forty minutes. From the station it is a short walk south along Station Road to the Square and All Saints' Church, or north to Minnis Bay and the clifftop bays. Margate is two stops east, via Westgate-on-Sea, and the Powell-Cotton Museum advertises itself as two train stops from Margate. Stagecoach buses also link Birchington with Westgate, Margate, Broadstairs, Canterbury and Herne Bay.
tips: Minnis Bay is roughly a 15-minute walk from the station.

name: Minnis Bay beach
summary: Long Blue Flag sandy bay with lifeguards, beach huts, a paddling pool and a restaurant; huge sands at low tide.
description: Minnis Bay is Birchington's main family beach, a long, open, rural-feeling sweep of sand with some shingle and rock, backed by stone steps and a promenade. At low tide the sand stretches a long way out; at high tide only a thin strip remains, and on spring tides the beach can vanish completely. It holds a combined Blue Flag and Seaside Award for 2026. Facilities include seasonal toilets, a beach shower, a picnic area, beach chalets for hire, a first aid point, a kiosk on the prom, a restaurant with a bar, a children's play area and a paddling pool that is good for crabbing. Windsurfing and kitesurfing are popular and the Minnis Bay Sailing Club, founded in 1950, is next to the beach. Coastguard cottages were built here in the 1870s and the first shops by the bay opened in 1903. In 2026 RNLI lifeguards patrolled 10:00-18:00 at weekends and bank holidays from 23 May to 17 July, then daily from 18 July to 6 September.
address: The Parade, Minnis Bay, Birchington, Kent
opening_hours: Open access. Council-listed toilet hours: Apr-Sep 08:00-21:00, Oct-Mar 08:00-17:40 (older council page).
dogs: Dogs banned from the main beach at all times 1 May - 30 September; welcome the rest of the year.
accessibility: Disabled parking; one beach wheelchair bookable through YourLeisure (03333 660 661); access statement on Visit Thanet.
tips: Check tide times: at high spring tides there is no beach. Barbecues only after 18:00. Visit Thanet calls parking free, an older council page says pay & display - check signs.

name: Minnis Bay play area & paddling pool
summary: Children's playground near the prom and a seawater paddling pool where kids hunt for crabs.
description: Just behind the beach at Minnis Bay is a children's play area, and on the foreshore is a paddling pool that refills with the tide. Visit Thanet describes the pool as a great spot for youngsters to look for crabs and other small sea creatures, and it gives children somewhere to splash about when the sea itself is far out across the sands. With the kiosk, toilets and restaurant close by, this end of the bay is the easiest base for a day out with small children. RNLI lifeguards cover the main beach in the summer season.
address: The Parade, Minnis Bay, Birchington, Kent
dogs: Dogs banned from the main beach 1 May - 30 September.
tips: Bring a bucket and net for crabbing; check the tide so the pool is uncovered.

name: The Minnis (bar & restaurant)
summary: Bar and restaurant right on the Minnis Bay promenade, owned by Kent brewer Shepherd Neame.
description: Standing at the end of The Parade above Minnis Bay, this bar and restaurant is the only proper sit-down eatery directly on the beach. The council notes that it is owned by Shepherd Neame, the Faversham brewery, and serves bar food, while Visit Thanet lists it simply as the bay's restaurant with a bar. Its terrace looks straight out over the bay and its sunsets to the west, towards Reculver's towers on the horizon. Walkers heading west along the Thanet coast and Wantsum sea wall often use it as a meeting point.
address: The Parade, Minnis Bay, Birchington, Kent
tips: Book ahead on sunny summer weekends.

name: Minnis Bay Bronze Age settlement site
summary: Foreshore site of a Late Bronze Age settlement that yielded a 73-piece bronze hoard now in the British Museum.
description: The sands of Minnis Bay hide one of Kent's most important prehistoric discoveries. A schoolboy, Jimmy Beck, first spotted ancient material on the foreshore, and in 1939 a Late Bronze Age settlement lying between the high and low tide lines was excavated. It had a rough rectangular hollow, seventeen storage pits and later timber structures, and produced the Minnis Bay founder's hoard of 73 bronze pieces, now in the British Museum. Earlier, in 1904, fourteen bronze axeheads were found in an earthenware bowl nearby. Antoinette Powell-Cotton also dug on the foreshore, and her finds are now in the Powell-Cotton Museum at Quex. Another record lists palstaves, socketed axes, a sword and a spear dated to around 1000-700 BC. The sea has since destroyed all visible trace of the settlement, so there is nothing to see on the beach today, but it is a striking thought while walking the sands at low tide.
tips: See the actual finds at the Powell-Cotton Museum, Quex Park.

name: Grenham Bay
summary: Quiet, partly sandy bay under chalk cliffs and sea stacks between Minnis Bay and Beresford Gap.
description: East of Minnis Bay the land rises and the shore turns into a series of small bays under white chalk cliffs. Grenham Bay is the first of these, a partly sandy beach with chalk stacks, its cliff foot protected by a sea wall and promenade that carries the Viking Coastal Trail. It is much quieter than Minnis Bay, with no listed beach facilities, and it forms part of the north-east Kent coast that is protected as a Site of Special Scientific Interest for its chalk habitats and birds. In winter the rocks and sands are good for spotting waders and Brent geese. At high tide the sea reaches the wall, so time your walk for falling or low water.
dogs: Listed by the Thanet Coast Project as a beach where dogs are welcome (no seasonal ban). Avoid high-tide bird roosts in winter.
accessibility: Reached by steps or slopes from the clifftop; promenade at the foot of the cliff.
tips: Walk along the sea-wall promenade from Minnis Bay at low tide.

name: Beresford Gap
summary: Small chalk-cliff bay in the centre of Birchington's coast, home of a wakeboard and water-ski club.
description: Beresford Gap is a cleft in the chalk cliffs between Grenham Bay and Epple Bay, giving access down to a small, partly sandy beach with chalk stacks and rocky foreshore. It sits directly north of the village centre, so it is the quickest way from the station area to the sea. Since 2004 it has been the home of the Beresford Wakeboard and Water Ski Club, so on calm summer days you may see boats and boarders offshore. Like its neighbours it lies within the protected north-east Kent coast and is crossed by the sea-wall promenade of the Viking Coastal Trail.
address: Beresford Gap, off The Parade / Cliff Road, Birchington, Kent
accessibility: Slipway/gap down from the clifftop; promenade along the cliff foot.
tips: A good point to join the promenade between Minnis Bay and Westgate.

name: Epple Bay
summary: Easternmost of Birchington's bays: a sandy cove under chalk cliffs, no facilities, popular with dog walkers.
description: Epple Bay is the last of Birchington's four bays before the coast continues to Westgate-on-Sea. It is a mostly sandy cove enclosed by chalk cliffs and stacks, reached from the clifftop by steps or a steep slope. There are no facilities on the beach, and at high tide the water comes right up to the sea wall, with rocks making it less suited to swimming. It is, however, a lovely spot for a quiet walk or for wildlife in winter and spring, when flocks of Brent geese and wading birds feed on the shore. The Viking Coastal Trail runs through the bay on the promenade, connecting west to Minnis Bay and east to Westgate and Margate.
address: Epple Bay Avenue area, Birchington, Kent
dogs: Listed by the Thanet Coast Project as a beach where dogs are welcome all year.
accessibility: Steps or steep slope from the clifftop.
tips: Go at low tide; nearest toilets and cafes are at Westgate's West Bay or Minnis Bay.

name: Plumpudding Island & the Northern Sea Wall
summary: Remote stretch of sea wall and marsh west of Minnis Bay, on the old Wantsum Channel, with wide views and wintering birds.
description: West of Minnis Bay the cliffs disappear and the coast becomes a long, straight sea wall protecting the flat marshes of the former Wantsum Channel. Plumpudding Island, despite the name, is a farm on the landward side of the wall, and it marks the point where walkers can turn inland towards St Nicholas-at-Wade or carry on along the wall towards Reculver's twin towers. The sea wall is surfaced and runs from Knock Point to Plumpudding, carrying both the Viking Coastal Trail and the Wantsum Walk. The mudflats and beach here are important for feeding and roosting birds; in 2026 Thanet District Council consulted on banning dogs all year from the beach and mudflats between Cold Harbour and Plum Pudding, with dogs on leads on the sea wall, after evidence of disturbance from Bird Wise East Kent. Check local signs for the rules in force when you visit.
address: Northern Sea Wall, west of Minnis Bay, Birchington, Kent
dogs: Proposed (2026 consultation): dogs excluded year-round from beach and mudflats between Cold Harbour and Plum Pudding, on leads on the sea wall. Final order not confirmed.
accessibility: Flat surfaced sea-wall path, exposed to wind.
tips: No facilities between Minnis Bay and Reculver; carry water. Great for cycling.

name: The Wantsum Channel & River Wantsum
summary: Marshland that was once a two-mile-wide sea strait making Thanet a real island; now a drainage ditch crossing the levels.
description: The flat grazing marshes between Birchington and Reculver were once open water. The Wantsum Channel was a strait about two miles wide separating the Isle of Thanet from the rest of Kent and joining the Thames Estuary with the English Channel. In Roman times it was a major shipping route, guarded by forts at each end: Regulbium at Reculver in the north and Rutupiae at Richborough in the south. Over the centuries shingle and silt choked the channel, a process sped up in the 12th and 13th centuries when monks reclaimed land, and by the 16th century it had dried up. What remains is the River Wantsum, little more than a drainage ditch running between Reculver and St Nicholas-at-Wade; an information board stands beside it on the sea wall. Village names such as St Nicholas-at-Wade recall the fords used to cross before the channel closed.
address: Wantsum marshes, between Reculver and Plumpudding, Kent
opening_hours: Open access along the sea wall
tips: Walk or cycle the sea wall from Minnis Bay to Reculver to cross the old channel.

name: Birchington Memorial Recreation Ground
summary: Village green given in 1923 by H. A. Erlebach in memory of his three sons killed in the First World War.
description: The Memorial Ground, south-east of the Square, is Birchington's main open green space. It was given to the village in 1923 by H. A. Erlebach in memory of his three sons, all killed in the First World War, and it is now owned by Thanet District Council. Today it is used for sports, dog walking and community events, and makes a pleasant break on a walk between the village centre and Quex Park.
tips: On the way between the Square and Quex Park.

name: Westgate & Birchington Golf Club
summary: Clifftop golf course between Birchington and Westgate with sea views.
description: Between Epple Bay and Westgate-on-Sea the clifftop is occupied by the Westgate and Birchington Golf Club, an 18-hole course according to Wikipedia's Birchington article, laid out along the edge of the chalk cliffs above the sea. The clubhouse is on Canterbury Road. The promenade below the cliffs and the coastal path give walkers sea views alongside the course.
tips: Contact the club directly about visitor rounds; details not verified.

name: Viking Coastal Trail: Reculver to Margate section
summary: Flat, mostly traffic-free sea-wall and promenade cycle route through Minnis Bay and Birchington's bays to Margate.
description: The Viking Coastal Trail (Regional Cycle Route 15) loops around the Isle of Thanet, keeping close to the coast from Reculver past Margate, Broadstairs, Ramsgate and Pegwell Bay before heading inland through Minster and St Nicholas-at-Wade. Published lengths vary from about 25 to 32 miles. The roughly nine-mile stretch between Reculver and Margate is widely described as the flattest and most traffic-free part. From Reculver's towers it follows the Wantsum sea wall past Plumpudding to Minnis Bay, then runs along the promenade at the foot of the chalk cliffs through Grenham Bay, Beresford Gap and Epple Bay to Westgate's West Bay and St Mildred's Bay, and on via Westbrook to Margate. It is open all year to walkers and cyclists, but some busy beach promenades restrict cycling in the summer season, so follow local signs between May and September.
address: Starts at Reculver Country Park; passes Minnis Bay, Birchington
dogs: Seasonal beach dog rules apply on the beaches it passes.
accessibility: Largely flat and surfaced along the coast.
tips: The promenade can be overtopped at high tide in rough weather; check tides before cycling below the cliffs.

name: Acol village
summary: Tiny hamlet south of Birchington that gave its name, via a London street, to the Acol bridge bidding system.
description: Acol is one of the smallest communities in Kent, a hamlet of under 300 people about a mile and a half south of Birchington, close to the western end of the former Manston runway. Its name appears in 1270 as Acholt, meaning oak wood. After the Napoleonic Wars local labourers suffered such hardship that many emigrated with help from their parishes. Around 1880 Henry Perry Cotton of Quex Park developed land in Kilburn, London, and named one of its streets Acol Road; in the 1930s members of the Acol Bridge Club there devised the Acol bidding system, still the standard in British bridge. Nearby is a chalk pit associated with a smuggling legend, retold by Richard Harris Barham in the Ingoldsby Legends, in which an exciseman and a smuggler die and are said to haunt the spot.
tips: Bridge players: a fun photo stop for the village sign.

name: St Mildred's Church, Acol
summary: Flint Gothic Revival church-and-school of 1876 designed by C. N. Beazley, with Gibbs & Howard glass.
description: Acol's little church was built in 1876 to serve as both a church and a school for the hamlet. It was designed by C. N. Beazley, the architect who also designed St Saviour's at Westgate-on-Sea and the reredos at Birchington's All Saints. Built of flint rubble in the Gothic Revival style, it has stained glass windows by the Victorian firm Gibbs & Howard. The church is small and simple, in keeping with a hamlet of only a few hundred people, and makes a quick stop when exploring the lanes south of Birchington towards Manston.

name: Monkton Nature Reserve
summary: 16-acre former chalk quarry turned wildlife reserve with orchids, butterflies, pond dipping and the UK's first artificial bat cave.
description: Run by the Thanet Countryside Trust charity, Monkton Nature Reserve occupies a 16-acre abandoned chalk quarry on the hills north of Monkton village that nature has reclaimed. Chalk grassland supports wildflowers and ten recorded species of orchid among more than 350 flowering plants, and some 25 species of butterfly. There is woodland over forty years old for birds, ponds for dipping, exposed chalk faces of geological interest, and what is described as the UK's first artificial bat cave. Families can follow trails, a sculpture hunt, nature bingo and brass rubbing. The Field Study Centre at the entrance has archaeological and natural history displays, second-hand books and gifts, and the Cabin cafe serves light refreshments. The site is also home to the Thanet Astronomical Observatory.
address: Canterbury Road, Monkton, near Ramsgate, Kent
opening_hours: Tue, Thu, Sat, Sun 10:00-16:00 (last entry 15:00); Fridays in school holidays only; closed bank holidays.
price: Adult £5, child 4-16 £2.50, under 4 free, family (2+2) £10 (Visit Thanet listing); Field Study Centre free.
accessibility: Ramp into the single-storey centre, accessible toilet; trails include about 15 steps and most are unsuitable for wheelchairs or buggies.
tips: Free car park; visit May-July for orchids and butterflies.

name: St Mary Magdalene Church, Monkton
summary: Smallest of Thanet's seven surviving ancient churches, on a Domesday site, rebuilt in the 15th century.
description: A church at Monkton is recorded in the Domesday survey, and the present building dates from the 12th century. It was largely remodelled in the 15th century, when the north porch was added, the tower raised, the north aisle blocked up, new windows put in and the roof built. It is the smallest of the seven ancient churches that survive on the Isle of Thanet. The churchyard is enclosed by stone walls with several gates. Monkton was historically the mother church of Birchington, whose All Saints began as a chapel under Monkton's care.
tips: Combine with Monkton Nature Reserve just north of the village.

name: St Nicholas Church, St Nicholas-at-Wade
summary: 13th-century flint church, once a chapel of Reculver, with 16th-century brasses and a 1615 carved pulpit.
description: The village church of St Nicholas is built of flint and dates from the 13th century. It began as a chapel of ease for St Mary's at Reculver, and its first recorded rector was Adam de Brancestre in 1294. The parish grew in 1310 when it absorbed the chapelry of All Saints at Shuart, and again in the mid-16th century when St Giles at Sarre was added. Inside are brasses from the 16th century, a carved oak pulpit dated 1615 and a royal coat of arms of George III. It now belongs to the Wantsum Benefice. The Viking Coastal Trail passes through the village on its inland leg.

name: St Nicholas-at-Wade village
summary: Village on the old Wantsum crossing, known for the Hoodening folk custom, two pubs and a medieval chapel under St Nicholas Court.
description: St Nicholas-at-Wade sits on the western edge of Thanet where, before the Wantsum and Stour channels silted up, travellers could wade across to the mainland. Roman shipbuilding remains have been reported between the village and Sarre. The village is best known for Hoodening, a Kentish form of mumming with a wooden horse's head, and folk groups including a border morris side still meet here. It was also long associated with potato growing. There are two pubs, The Bell and The Sun, plus a post office and a village hall dating from 1930. St Nicholas Court, a private property, has a medieval underground chapel of uncertain origin that is occasionally opened to visitors.
tips: A lunch stop on the inland leg of the Viking Coastal Trail.

name: Sarre Windmill
summary: Grade II listed 1820 smock mill on a brick base, restored 1986-91; now a private holiday let, view from outside.
description: Sarre Windmill was built in 1820 by the Canterbury millwright John Holman. It is a three-storey, eight-sided smock mill standing on a two-storey brick base, with four double patent sails. Wind drove it until 1920, when its sails were moved to another mill, after which a gas engine powered it until milling stopped in 1940. After years as a semi-derelict building it was restored between 1986 and 1991. It is Grade II listed. Since 2011 it has been used as a holiday let and Wikipedia records it as closed to visitors, so enjoy it as a landmark from the road through Sarre, the village at the old southern crossing of the Wantsum.
opening_hours: Not open to the public (exterior view only)
tips: Photograph it from the roadside; it is private.

name: Reculver Towers & Roman Fort
summary: Free English Heritage site: twin 12th-century church towers inside a Roman Saxon Shore fort, a landmark seen from Birchington.
description: The twin towers at Reculver are visible all along the coast from Minnis Bay. The Romans built a small fort here during the conquest of AD 43 and, from the late 2nd century, a larger stone fort called Regulbium that later formed part of the Saxon Shore defences guarding the northern mouth of the Wantsum Channel; it was abandoned in the 370s. Around 669 King Ecgberht of Kent granted the site for a monastery dedicated to St Mary, and King Eadberht II was buried here in the 760s. The monastic church became the parish church, and its twin towers were added in a 12th-century rebuilding. As the sea ate away the cliff and the village was deserted, the church was demolished from 1809, a decision later condemned as vandalism. Trinity House bought the remains in 1810 to keep the towers as a sea mark and built groynes to protect them. Parts of the Roman walls survive around the ruins.
address: Reculver Lane, Reculver, near Herne Bay, Kent
opening_hours: Exterior any reasonable time in daylight; North Tower interior on selected days April-October (see English Heritage).
accessibility: Grounds reached by a long slope from the car park.
tips: Paid public car park (not English Heritage); toilets and cafe in the country park. Walk or cycle here along the sea wall from Minnis Bay (about 5 km).

name: Reculver Country Park & Visitor Centre
summary: Clifftop country park around the towers with a visitor centre, Roman-themed play park, shingle beach and birdwatching.
description: Reculver Country Park wraps around the towers on the low cliffs east of Herne Bay and draws over 200,000 visitors a year. Most of it lies within the Bishopstone Cliffs Local Nature Reserve, and the coast is protected as an SSSI, Special Protection Area and Ramsar site. In winter thousands of migrating birds use the shore, and in summer sand martins nest in the soft cliffs. The shingle beach is popular for fossil hunting, and there is a Roman-inspired children's play park that is open all year. The visitor centre beside the towers reopened in 2009 as a renewable energy and interpretation centre about the area's history and wildlife. The park is a meeting point of routes: the Viking Coastal Trail starts here, and the Wantsum Walk and Oyster Bay Trail connect towards Herne Bay.
address: Reculver Lane, Reculver, near Herne Bay, Kent
opening_hours: Park open access; visitor centre and cafe hours not confirmed.
tips: Toilets and a cafe are in the country park. Good spot for sunset and winter birdwatching.

name: Bishopstone Cliffs & Glen
summary: 67-hectare clifftop nature reserve west of Reculver with grassland, sand martin colonies and skylarks.
description: Bishopstone Cliffs is a 67-hectare Local Nature Reserve owned and managed by Canterbury City Council, most of it inside Reculver Country Park. It is part of the Thanet Coast SSSI and the Thanet Coast and Sandwich Bay Ramsar site and Special Protection Area. The clifftop grassland supports rare insects, while sand martins dig nest holes in the soft sandy cliffs. Listen for skylarks, meadow pipits and corn buntings. Bishopstone Glen is a small wooded stream valley cutting down to the shore at the western end, from which a walk east along the clifftop leads to Reculver's towers.
address: Bishopstone Lane, near Herne Bay, Kent
tips: Keep away from the crumbling cliff edge.

name: King Ethelbert Inn, Reculver
summary: Historic pub beside Reculver's towers, on the Viking Coastal Trail, with a terrace and children's play area.
description: The King Ethelbert stands in the country park just below the Reculver Towers and the Roman fort walls. An inn called the Hoy and Anchor stood here earlier and was rebuilt and renamed the King Ethelbert by around 1838-1843. Today it serves real ale, usually including at least one beer from a Kent brewery, and good-value food including Sunday roasts, with a shellfish stall in summer. There is a sunny terrace and a children's play area in the garden, making it a natural stop for walkers and cyclists at the start or end of the Viking Coastal Trail.

name: Reculver bouncing bomb test range
summary: In 1943 Barnes Wallis's bouncing bombs were test-dropped off Reculver before the Dambusters raid.
description: The shallow sea off Reculver played a secret part in the Second World War. In April and May 1943 inert prototypes of Barnes Wallis's bouncing bombs were dropped here by aircraft flying from RAF Manston, at first a Vickers Wellington, later with pilots of No. 617 Squadron loading inert mines at Manston, while modified Mosquitoes dropped the smaller Highball. Early versions shattered their outer casings on hitting the water, which led Wallis to drop the spherical casing from Upkeep; the operational weapon was used in the Dambusters raid of May 1943. Prototypes have since been recovered from the sea here: remains of an Upkeep found in 1997 are at Herne Bay Museum, and a Highball core is on show at the Spitfire and Hurricane Memorial Museum at Manston. Standing by the towers, you look out over the old test range.
address: Reculver seafront, near Herne Bay, Kent
tips: See a recovered Highball at the Spitfire & Hurricane Memorial Museum, Manston.

name: Spitfire & Hurricane Memorial Museum
summary: Free museum on the old RAF Manston airfield displaying a Spitfire XVI and Hurricane IIc, with a cafe and memorial garden.
description: On the north side of the former RAF Manston airfield, this free museum is built around two famous fighters: Supermarine Spitfire Mk XVI TB752 and Hawker Hurricane Mk IIc LF751. Around them are Second World War displays, a Spitfire combat record, information on the pilots and objects about life in and around Ramsgate during the war, including a recovered Highball bouncing-bomb core from the Reculver trials. Manston itself opened in 1916 and was heavily bombed in the Battle of Britain in 1940. Outside is the Allied Crew Memorial Garden. Paid extras include a Spitfire flight experience in a cockpit simulator and a Lancaster flight simulator. The museum is a registered charity and has been a registered museum since 1991.
address: The Memorial Museum, Manston Road, Manston, near Ramsgate, Kent
opening_hours: Visit Thanet lists daily 10:00-16:00; other listings give longer summer hours. Check the museum website.
price: Free (donations welcome). Spitfire flight experience £30/30 min; Lancaster simulator £75/30 min (Mon-Wed, phone to book).
dogs: Assistance dogs welcome; other dogs not stated.
accessibility: Entirely level museum, wheelchair and scooter friendly; one wheelchair to borrow; accessible unisex toilet; two accessible parking bays.
tips: Free car park; the RAF Manston History Museum is next door.

name: RAF Manston History Museum
summary: Volunteer-run museum of Manston airfield's history, with aircraft including a Canberra, Vulcan cockpit and Victor cockpit.
description: Next to the Spitfire and Hurricane museum, the RAF Manston History Museum tells the story of the airfield from its opening in 1916 as an Admiralty aerodrome, through heavy bombing in the Battle of Britain, the 1943 bouncing-bomb trials and the US Air Force's Cold War years in 1952-58, to the RAF's departure in 1999 and the later commercial airport. Highlights include an English Electric Canberra, the cockpit section of Avro Vulcan XA893 and the cockpit of Handley Page Victor K.2 XL190, alongside vehicles, uniforms and memorabilia. The NAAFI Cafe serves refreshments, and the museum runs themed event days such as open cockpits.
opening_hours: Summer: daily 10:00-16:00 (last entry 15:15). Winter: Mon-Fri 10:00-15:00 (last entry 14:15), Sat-Sun 10:00-16:00. Subject to volunteer availability.
price: Adult £7, child under 16 £3.50, under 5 free, concession £6, carer £4, family (2+4) £20.
tips: Visit both Manston museums in one trip; they share the same road.

name: Westgate-on-Sea
summary: Genteel Victorian resort between Birchington and Margate, with two sandy bays, a historic cinema and a WWI seaplane past.
description: Until the 1860s Westgate was little more than a farm, a coastguard station of 1791 and a few cottages by St Mildred's Bay. Developers then laid it out as a select resort, and the railway station opened in 1871; by 1901 almost 2,800 people lived here. A Roman villa was found in the early 20th century where Beach Road now runs. The artist Louis Wain, famous for his cat pictures, lived in Westgate from 1890 to 1917, first in Adrian Square. Other residents included surgeon Sir Erasmus Wilson and astronomer Norman Lockyer. Today the town's attractions are its two beaches, West Bay and St Mildred's Bay, the clifftop promenade, St Saviour's Church and the Carlton Cinema in the former town hall. It is one stop east of Birchington by train.
tips: Walk the promenade from Epple Bay into Westgate (about 2 km).

name: St Mildred's Bay
summary: Westgate's larger sandy bay with promenade, tidal pool, cafes, beach huts and summer lifeguards; once a WWI seaplane base.
description: St Mildred's Bay is the bigger of Westgate's two beaches, a cliff-lined sandy bay with a promenade and a tidal pool. Only a thin strip of sand remains at high tide and the beach is covered on spring tides. Along the prom are tennis courts, cafes and bars, and beach huts can be hired. It holds a Seaside Award for 2026. In August 1914 the Royal Naval Air Service opened a seaplane base here to defend the Thames Estuary towns, followed by a landplane base at Manston in 1916. Facilities include seasonal toilets and a disabled toilet, with parking close by. In 2026 RNLI lifeguards patrolled daily from 18 July to 6 September, 10:00-18:00.
dogs: Dogs not allowed 10:00-18:00 from 1 May to 30 September; welcome outside those hours and in winter.
accessibility: Disabled access to the beach and disabled toilet; access statement on Visit Thanet.
tips: Go around low tide for space; barbecues only after 18:00.

name: West Bay, Westgate-on-Sea
summary: Fully tidal sandy bay with rock pools, a cafe and pub nearby, beach huts and summer lifeguards.
description: West Bay is the smaller of Westgate's two beaches, a completely tidal sandy bay framed by chalk cliffs. At low tide it is ideal for sandcastles, and the rocks at either side are good for rock pooling. A promenade cafe and restaurant, a beach shop and a pub across the road cover refreshments, and beach chalets can be hired. It holds a Seaside Award for 2026. Toilets are seasonal according to Visit Thanet (the council describes a block open all year with seasonal hours). In 2026 RNLI lifeguards patrolled daily from 18 July to 6 September, 10:00-18:00. Sea Road has on-street parking and Westgate station is a short walk away.
dogs: Dogs not allowed 10:00-18:00 from 1 May to 30 September.
accessibility: One beach wheelchair bookable via YourLeisure (03333 660 661); access statement on Visit Thanet.
tips: Bring nets for the rock pools at low tide.

name: St Saviour's Church, Westgate-on-Sea
summary: Victorian parish church of 1884 by C. N. Beazley, whose bells include medieval ones from Canterbury.
description: St Saviour's was built in 1884 for the young resort of Westgate, to designs by the architect C. N. Beazley, who also worked at Birchington and Acol. In 1975 it received five historic bells from the redundant Holy Cross Church in Canterbury, among them one from the 14th century and three from the early 17th century, so this Victorian church holds bells far older than the building itself. The church stands in the centre of the planned resort, a few streets back from the seafront, close to the Carlton Cinema and the station, and makes a short stop on a stroll around Westgate's Victorian streets.
tips: A few minutes' walk from the Carlton Cinema.

name: Carlton Cinema, Westgate-on-Sea
summary: Grade II listed 1910 former town hall turned cinema in 1912, still showing films; 1987 Cinema of the Year.
description: Westgate's cinema occupies a flamboyant building finished in 1910 as the town hall, a mix of styles that architectural historian John Newman called an extraordinary jumble of motifs. Within two years it had become the Town Hall Cinema, and in the 1930s it was renamed the Carlton. It won the British cinema industry's Cinema of the Year award in 1987 and is Grade II listed as part of the terrace at 25-35 St Mildred's Road. Still privately run, it now operates as a multi-screen picture house showing new releases, with sensory-friendly, baby-friendly and subtitled screenings.
opening_hours: Box office staffed weekdays after 14:00, weekends after 11:00; see website for screenings.
accessibility: Accessibility page on the cinema website; sensory and supportive-environment screenings offered.
tips: A good rainy-evening option.

name: Adrian Square (Louis Wain's Westgate)
summary: Small Victorian garden square where the cat artist Louis Wain first lived during his 27 years in Westgate.
description: Louis Wain, the Victorian and Edwardian illustrator whose anthropomorphic cats made him famous, lived in Westgate-on-Sea from 1890 until 1917. He first settled in Adrian Square, one of the small garden squares laid out when the resort was developed, and later moved to Collinwood Terrace, now part of Westgate Bay Avenue. Wikipedia notes that the exact dates of his moves are inconsistent between sources. The square is a quiet spot just back from the seafront between the station and St Mildred's Bay.

name: Westbrook Bay
summary: Sandy family bay on Margate's western edge with lifeguards, adventure golf, beach huts and a water-ski zone.
description: Westbrook Bay is the first sandy beach you reach heading east from Westgate into Margate. It is a family beach with a designated water-ski area, and a small section of sand stays dry even at high tide. Along the promenade is the Strokes adventure golf course, with tennis courts and bowls nearby, and the Westbrook Loggia on the lower promenade. It holds a Seaside Award for 2026. Facilities include seasonal toilets and disabled toilets, beach chalets for hire, a gift shop and a cafe. The chargeable Barnes car park lies just to the west on the lower promenade. In 2026 RNLI lifeguards patrolled at weekends and bank holidays from 23 May to 17 July and daily from 18 July to 6 September, 10:00-18:00.
dogs: Dogs must be on a lead 10:00-18:00 from 1 May to 30 September.
accessibility: Disabled access to the beach; one beach wheelchair bookable via YourLeisure (03333 660 661).
tips: A dog-friendlier alternative to Margate Main Sands in summer (leads required in the daytime).

name: Royal Sea Bathing Hospital (former)
summary: Pioneering 1791 sea-air hospital founded by Quaker doctor John Coakley Lettsom, now converted to apartments.
description: Above Westbrook Bay stands the long classical frontage of the Royal Sea Bathing Hospital, founded in 1791 by the Quaker physician and philanthropist Dr John Coakley Lettsom to treat scrofula, a form of tuberculosis, with fresh air, sunshine and sea bathing. It became one of the earliest specialist orthopaedic hospitals in Britain and went on treating tuberculosis until the early 1950s. Around 1880 Sir Erasmus Wilson, the surgeon who also lived in Westgate, funded an enlargement with a new ward, a heated salt-water pool and a chapel. The main building, chapel, mortuary and a statue of Wilson are Grade II listed. The whole complex has been converted into apartments, so it is a building to admire from the outside.
tips: Look for the statue of Erasmus Wilson outside.

name: Margate Main Sands
summary: Margate's big sandy town beach by the station, lifeguarded daily all summer; no dogs May-September.
description: Margate Main Sands is the broad, sheltered sandy beach right in front of the town, close to Margate railway station. It is the most lifeguarded beach in this part of Thanet: in 2026 RNLI lifeguards patrolled daily from 23 May to 6 September, 10:00-18:00. Public toilets are at the station end. It is a short train ride from Birchington (via Westgate) and an easy add-on to a day exploring Margate's old town, Dreamland and the seafront.
address: Marine Terrace / Margate seafront, Margate, Kent
dogs: Dogs not allowed at any time from 1 May to 30 September.
tips: Barbecues allowed only after 18:00 on Thanet beaches.

name: Northdown Park
summary: Public park around Georgian Northdown House, with walled gardens, a rock-garden dell, woodland and a play area.
description: Northdown Park, on the eastern side of Margate towards Cliftonville, is laid out around Northdown House, a Georgian mansion. The estate was sold to the council in 1939 on condition that it stay a public park. Close to the house are two enclosed gardens: the walled Frank Mathews Memorial Garden, planted around a paved sunken pool, and the Dell with its rock garden. The rest is open grassland with groups of trees and sports pitches, while the northern end has more natural woodland and a children's play area. An old nursery in the south-east corner is used by a Thanet Mind gardening project and is only occasionally open. The house itself is run by Your Leisure and hired for weddings and events. A café was not confirmed.
tips: Best combined with a Margate or Cliftonville visit; about 10 km from Birchington.
